div.head: CHAPTER 1. OVERVIEW OF THE TOPIC 1.1 Reasons for Choosing the Topic
div.p: In the era of digital transformation, information technology plays a pivotal role in every aspect of life. The demand for dynamic and interactive web applications is rapidly increasing, creating significant opportunities for web developers. We believe that AJAX (Asynchronous JavaScript and XML) is an ideal choice to embark on the journey of becoming proficient web developers.

Firstly, AJAX -a widely adopted technique -enables asynchronous content updates, as seen in popular platforms like Gmail, Google Maps, and live comment systems on social media. Mastering AJAX helps us integrate seamlessly into the job market, offering attractive career prospects and growth opportunities in web development.

Moreover, AJAX is recognized as an accessible technology to learn, with abundant free online resources, high practical applicability, and built-in features that facilitate the development of diverse web applications-from basic to advancedquickly and efficiently, saving both time and cost.
For these reasons, we believe that exploring AJAX will provide the essential knowledge needed to pave the way for a successful career in web development.

div.head: Objectives of the Topic
div.p: This project aims to thoroughly understand the core concepts of AJAX, including its asynchronous mechanisms, and to apply them in a practical setting. We will focus on the Fetch API for client-side requests, PHP for server-side processing, and MySQL for database management.

Additionally, the project will guide us in implementing a Live comment system using AJAX, honing our JavaScript and PHP programming skills, as well as our logical thinking. Ultimately, we will develop a simple live comment system with AJAX, gaining hands-on experience and evaluating the potential of this technology in enhancing real-time web interactions.

div.head: Principles of Operation
div.p: AJAX operates by leveraging several core technologies:
-JavaScript: Executes client-side logic to initiate asynchronous requests.
Two primary methods are used: XMLHttpRequest, the traditional approach, and Fetch API, a modern alternative offering a simpler syntax and Promise-based handling.

-XML/JSON: Data formats for exchanging information between client and server. While AJAX originally used XML, JSON is now more common due to its lightweight structure and ease of parsing in JavaScript.

-HTTP Requests: AJAX sends HTTP requests (e.g., GET, POST) to the server to Fetch or send data. For example, in our system, a POST request sends a new comment to the server, and a GET request retrieves updated comments.

The process begins when a user action (e.g., submitting a comment) triggers a JavaScript function. This function uses Fetch API to send an HTTP request to the server, which processes the request (via PHP in our case) and returns data (e.g., JSON). JavaScript then updates the DOM to display the new content without a page refresh. The following diagram illustrates this workflow:

div.head: Advantages and Challenges
div.p: AJAX offers significant benefits but also presents challenges:

div.head: Advantages Challenges
div.p: Reduced Server Load: Fetches only necessary data, minimizing bandwidth usage.

div.head: Handling Asynchronous Code:
div.p: Non-linear execution can complicate logic and state management.

div.head: Faster User Interactions:
div.p: Enables real-time updates, as seen in our live comment system.

div.head: Debugging Issues:
div.p: Asynchronous requests are harder to trace, especially with nested callbacks.

div.head: Definition of Fetch API
div.p: Fetch API is a modern JavaScript interface for making HTTP requests, introduced as a replacement for XMLHttpRequest. It provides a more flexible and Promise-based approach, simplifying asynchronous operations. In our project, Fetch API is used to send and receive comment data between the client and server.

div.head: Role in Asynchronous Web Development
div.p: Fetch API plays a crucial role in AJAX by enabling asynchronous HTTP requests with cleaner syntax and better error handling. It supports methods like GET and POST, and handles responses in formats like JSON. For example, in our live comment system, Fetch API sends a POST request to submit a comment and a GET request to retrieve new comments, ensuring real-time updates without page reloads.
Its Promise-based nature also makes it easier to manage asynchronous workflows compared to XMLHttpRequest.

div.head: PHP in Backend Development
div.p: PHP is a server-side scripting language widely used for web development. In our project, PHP handles backend logic, processing AJAX requests from the client.
For instance, when a user submits a comment, PHP receives the data via a POST request, validates it, and stores it in the database, returning a response to the client.

div.head: MySQL in Database Management
div.p: MySQL is an open-source relational database management system (DBMS) used to store and manage data. In our live comment system, MySQL stores user comments in a structured table, with fields like comment ID, user ID, content, and timestamp. PHP interacts with MySQL to insert new comments and retrieve existing ones, enabling persistent data storage for our application.

div.head: System Architecture
div.p: The system architecture for our live comment system follows a client-server model. The client (browser) uses HTML, CSS, and JavaScript (with Fetch API) to create the frontend interface and handle AJAX requests. The server, powered by PHP and MySQL, processes these requests, manages the database, and returns responses.

This architecture ensures efficient data flow and real-time updates, as depicted in a diagram (to be included in the final report). -AJAX is ideal for our live comment system because it allows the client to request new comments periodically (e.g., via Fetch API) without maintaining a constant connection. However, it introduces HTTP overhead, making it less efficient for high-frequency updates.

div.p: -WebSocket excels in scenarios requiring continuous, two-way communication, such as chat applications or online gaming, but its setup is more complex and resource-intensive.
-Server-Sent Events are suitable for server-driven updates, like live notifications, but lack the flexibility of AJAX for client-initiated requests.
For our project, AJAX strikes a balance between simplicity and functionality, making it the preferred choice for a live comment system with moderate real-time requirements.

div.head: User-Friendly Interface:
div.p: The frontend uses Bootstrap for responsive design, custom CSS for styling (e.g., comment highlighting with animations), and JavaScript for dynamic updates, ensuring an engaging user experience.
This system showcases how AJAX can enhance web applications by enabling asynchronous communication, making it an ideal case study for understanding realtime web interactions.

div.head: System Architecture
div.p: The Live Comment System follows a client-server architecture, with distinct roles for the frontend, backend, and communication layer: comments (for comments) and users (for user accounts).
 Communication Layer: Fetch API facilitates asynchronous HTTP requests between the client and server, using JSON as the data format. All API responses follow a consistent structure:

{ "success": true, "message": "Comment added successfully", "comment_id": 1 }  Data Flow: When a user submits a comment, the browser sends a POST request to the appropriate endpoint (add_comment.php or add_comment_auth.php).

The server validates the input, stores the comment in MySQL, and returns a JSON response. The browser then updates the DOM to display the new comment. Polling ensures continuous updates, and notifications (for authenticated users) alert users to new activity. This architecture ensures efficient data flow, scalability, and responsiveness, with Fetch API providing a modern, Promise-based approach to AJAX that simplifies asynchronous operations and error handling.

PHP: Manages API endpoints in the api/ directory, each handling specific functionality: 1. get_comments.php: Retrieves up to 20 comments newer than the specified last_id, ordered by id in descending order: // Get the last comment ID from the request (if any) $lastId = isset($_GET['last_id']) ? (int)$_GET['last_id'] : 0; try { // Prepare SQL statement to get comments newer than the last ID // Order by ID descending to get newest first if ($lastId > 0) { $stmt = $pdo->prepare("SELECT * FROM comments WHERE id > :last_id ORDER BY id DESC LIMIT 20"); $stmt->bindParam(':last_id', $lastId, PDO::PARAM_INT); } else { // If no last ID provided, get the most recent comments $stmt = $pdo->prepare("SELECT * FROM comments ORDER BY id DESC LIMIT 20"); } // Execute the statement $stmt->execute(); // Fetch all comments $comments = $stmt->FetchAll(PDO::FETCH_ASSOC); // Return success response with comments3. login.php: Authenticates users by verifying their username or email and password, setting session variables upon successful login. 4. register.php: Allows new users to register by validating their username, email, and password, hashing the password, and storing the user in the database. update_profile.php: Enables authenticated users to update their username, ensuring the new username is unique. 6. change_password.php: Allows authenticated users to change their password after verifying the current password. 7. logout.php: Terminates the user session and redirects to the homepage. MySQL: Stores data in a relational database named livecmt_db, with two primary tables: comments: Stores comments with fields id (auto-incremented primary key), username (VARCHAR(100)), content (TEXT), and created_at (TIMESTAMP).

note.p: 3.1 History and EvolutionAJAX emerged in the late 1990s but was formally named by Jesse James Garrett in his 2005 article, "Ajax: A New Approach to Web Applications." The concept originated with Microsoft's introduction of the XMLHttpRequest object in Internet Explorer 5, which allowed JavaScript to make asynchronous HTTP requests. This innovation marked a shift from static web pages to dynamic, interactive applications. Early adopters like Google leveraged AJAX in products such as Gmail and Google Maps, demonstrating its potential to revolutionize user experiences.Over the years, AJAX evolved significantly. The introduction of jQuery in 2006 simplified AJAX implementation by abstracting complex XMLHttpRequest operations. More recently, the Fetch API, introduced in 2015, replaced XMLHttpRequest with a modern, Promise-based approach, offering cleaner syntax and better error handling. Today, AJAX is a cornerstone of single-page applications (SPAs) and real-time systems, with JSON largely replacing XML as the preferred data format due to its lightweight nature.3.2 Comparison with Other Technologies (WebSocket, Server-SentEvents)AJAX is one of several technologies for real-time web communication, but it differs from alternatives like WebSocket and Server-Sent Events (SSE) in implementation and use cases. div.head: Database Schema
div.p: The Live Comment System uses a MySQL database named livecmt_db with two primary tables: comments for storing comments and users for managing user accounts.

div.head: Database Connection (config.php)
div.p: The config.php script establishes a connection to the MySQL database using PDO, ensuring secure and efficient database interactions:

$host = 'localhost'; $dbname = 'livecmt_db'; $username = 'root'; $password = ''; try { $pdo = new PDO("mysql:host=$host;dbname=$dbname", $username, $password); $pdo->setAttribute(PDO::ATTR_ERRMODE, PDO::ERRMODE_EXCEPTION); } catch(PDOException $e) { die("ERROR: Could not connect. " . $e->getMessage()); }

div.head: Comment Posting (add_comment_auth.php)
div.p: The add_comment_auth.php endpoint handles comment posting for authenticated users, ensuring only logged-in users can post comments: This script validates the session, ensures the comment content is provided and within length limits, and inserts the comment into the comments table using PDO prepared statements to prevent SQL injection.

div.head: Fetching Comments (get_comments.php)
div.p: The get_comments.php endpoint retrieves comments for display, accessible to both authenticated and unauthenticated users: This endpoint supports polling by Fetching comments newer than the specified last_id, limiting the response to 20 comments to optimize performance.

div.head: User Authentication (login.php)
div.p: The login.php endpoint authenticates users by verifying their credentials: This script supports login with either a username or email, verifies the password using password_verify(), and sets session variables for authenticated users.

div.head: Backend Implementation
div.p: The frontend is implemented using HTML, CSS, and JavaScript, with a focus on the authenticated user experience in dashboard.php.

div.head: Testing Overview
div.p: The Live Comment System was rigorously tested to ensure its functionality, reliability, performance, and usability meet the project requirements. The testing process focused on verifying core features, including user authentication, comment posting, real-time comment updates, and notifications, while also evaluating the system's performance under various conditions and its usability for end users.

div.head: The testing methodology included:
div.p:  Functional Testing: To verify that each feature (e.g., login, registration, comment posting, notifications) works as expected.
 Performance Testing: To assess the system's response time, scalability, and resource usage under different loads.
 Security Testing: To identify potential vulnerabilities, such as SQL injection or cross-site scripting (XSS), and ensure the system is secure.
Testing was conducted in a local development environment using XAMPP (Apache, MySQL) on a Windows machine with 8GB RAM and a 2.4 GHz processor.
The browser used for testing was Google Chrome (version 120.0), ensuring compatibility with modern web standards.

div.head: Functional Testing
div.p: Functional testing was performed to verify that each component of the Live Comment System works as intended. Test cases were designed to cover the main features: user authentication, comment posting, real-time updates, and notifications.
Below are the key test cases and their results.

div.head: Conclusion:
div.p: The Live Comment System is secure against common web vulnerabilities, thanks to the use of prepared statements, input escaping, and session management. However, additional measures, such as implementing CSRF tokens for form submissions and enabling HTTPS in production, could further enhance security.

div.head: Evaluation Summary
div.p: The testing and evaluation process confirmed that the Live Comment System meets its design goals and performs well across various dimensions:
 Functionality: All core features-user authentication, comment posting, realtime updates, and notifications-work as intended, with all functional test cases passing (Section 6.2).
 Performance: The system handles moderate loads (up to 50 concurrent users)
with acceptable response times (15-32 ms) and resource usage (Section 6.3).
For larger-scale deployment, optimizations like database indexing and caching are recommended.
 Security: The system is secure against common threats like SQL injection, XSS, and session hijacking, thanks to robust security practices (Section 6.5).
Additional measures like CSRF protection and HTTPS are suggested for production.

Overall Assessment: The Live Comment System is a functional, performant, and user-friendly web application that successfully demonstrates the use of AJAX for real-time commenting. While the system is ready for small-scale deployment, scaling to larger user bases will require performance optimizations and additional security measures.
